headline: Desert Storm begins; oil falls by a third and stocks leap
text: After the UN's deadline of 15 January for Iraq to leave Kuwait passed, a US-led coalition of more than 40 countries began bombing Iraq and Iraqi forces in Kuwait on 17 January. Iraq has fired Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia. On the first day of the air war the oil price fell by about a third and the S&P 500 rose 3.7 percent.
imageCaption: US troops during Operation Desert Storm, 1991

headline: Kuwait is free after a hundred hours of ground war
text: The attack on the ground began on 24 February and ended after one hundred hours: on 28 February President Bush declared a ceasefire, with Kuwait freed and Iraq's army driven out. A coalition of 42 countries with more than 950,000 soldiers took part. Retreating Iraqi troops set fire to more than six hundred Kuwaiti oil wells.
imageCaption: Kuwaiti oil fires, 1991

headline: Hopes of peace in the Gulf lift shares
text: Stock markets rose in February as the Gulf war neared its end, after Iraq said it was ready, under conditions, to leave Kuwait.
source: Die Zeit, 'Markt-Report: Spekulation auf Frieden', 22 February 1991, https://www.zeit.de/1991/09/spekulation-auf-frieden (read 2026-10-03); Die Zeit, 'Markt-Report: Jubel-Hausse blieb aus', 1 March 1991, https://www.zeit.de/1991/10/jubel-hausse-blieb-aus (read 2026-10-03); data/out/bmw.json (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Frankfurt Stock Exchange building

headline: Wal-Mart overtakes Sears as America's largest retailer
text: Sears reported 1990 sales of 31.99 billion dollars for its stores business, knocking it off the top spot it had held since about 1900. Wal-Mart, with 1990 sales of 32.6 billion dollars, is now the country's largest retailer, and Kmart, at 32.07 billion, also passed Sears.
imageCaption: Sam Walton, in his Wal-Mart cap and name badge, talks with an associate on a store visit

headline: McDonald's tries a low-fat burger
text: McDonald's is introducing the McLean Deluxe, a hamburger with a patty that is 91% fat-free, to win health-conscious customers. Abroad, McDonald's now runs more than 3,600 restaurants in 58 countries, and 37% of systemwide sales come from outside the United States.
source: https://www.company-histories.com/McDonalds-Corporation-Company-History.html (read 2026-10-03; the month of launch is not given there, only the year 1991)
imageCaption: Muscovites queue at the McDonald's on Pushkin Square in Moscow, 1991

headline: Apple shares fall 15%: cheap Macs sell, but the profit on each is thin
text: Apple shares fell 15% in May after a 19% fall in April. The low-priced Macintosh Classic and LC are selling, but Apple earns far less on each one, and the company said it would offset the lower gross margins by cutting operating expenses. Reports in mid-May spoke of 600 to 2,000 of the 15,600 jobs going, mostly in administration; Apple would not confirm a figure.
imageCaption: The Macintosh LC, introduced in October 1990

headline: Apple cuts about 1,500 jobs; shares down 39% since March
text: Apple announced the cuts investors had been waiting for: about 1,500 jobs, a tenth of its staff, to bring costs in line with the thinner profits of its cheaper Macintosh models. The shares fell another 12% in June and have lost 39% since March, in a month when the whole market fell 5%. Apple remains profitable; the question is how much it can earn selling computers at 1,000 dollars instead of 2,500.
source: SFGate "Apple layoffs: Painful but necessary" and Post-Bulletin, via search summaries (pages did not load) (read 2026-10-03); Seattle Times 1991-05-18 for the staff total; price changes from data/out/aapl.json
imageCaption: John Sculley, Apple's chief executive

headline: LDDS shares have quadrupled in eighteen months
text: Shares of LDDS have roughly quadrupled since the start of 1990 as the company keeps buying smaller long-distance companies.
imageCaption: Jackson, Mississippi, 2018

headline: Apple and IBM, enemies for a decade, agree to work together
text: On 3 July Apple and IBM signed a letter of intent for an alliance that would have been unthinkable a few years ago: a new family of microprocessors with Motorola, derived from IBM's POWER chips, a joint company to build a next-generation operating system from Apple's "Pink" project, and another for multimedia software. The aim is a common platform that other makers can build on, a direct challenge to the Microsoft-and-Intel world of the PC. Apple shares rose 11% in July.
imageCaption: An IBM PS/2 personal computer, IBM's PC line of the time

headline: The World Wide Web opens to the internet: there is one website
text: On 23 August Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web, a system of linked pages developed at the CERN physics laboratory in Geneva, was made available to the whole internet. The internet itself still links mainly universities and research labs. There is nothing to surf yet: no shops, no newspapers, no search engines, no pictures. The internet is a way for scientists to send each other messages and files, and almost nobody outside the universities has heard of it.
imageCaption: The NeXT computer that served as the first web server at CERN, Geneva, where Tim Berners-Lee built the World Wide Web in 1990-91

headline: Hardliners try a coup in Moscow and fail
text: On 19 August eight hardliners, among them Vice President Gennady Yanayev, KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov, announced that they had taken power, saying Mikhail Gorbachev was unable to govern; he was held at his holiday home in Crimea, a day before he was to sign a new union treaty giving the republics more power. Tanks came into Moscow, but Russia's president Boris Yeltsin climbed onto one outside the Russian parliament and called for resistance; three civilians were killed on 21 August, and the coup collapsed. Gorbachev gave up the leadership of the Communist Party on 24 August, the day Ukraine declared independence; Estonia and Latvia had declared theirs during the coup.
imageCaption: 1991 Soviet coup attempt, 1991

headline: Cisco's sales more than double again
text: Cisco closed its fiscal year at the end of July with sales of $183 million, up from $70 million the year before, and net income of $43 million. Demand for routers that tie together company networks of different makes keeps growing faster than the company can hire.
imageCaption: Cisco's IGS multiprotocol router/bridge of about 1990, the compact router behind the early-1990s sales growth, with the old Cisco Systems logo

headline: The Onoue scandal: IBJ lent billions to a restaurant owner
text: On 8 August forged deposit certificates worth 342 billion yen issued to Nui Onoue, the owner of an Osaka restaurant, came to light; she was arrested on 13 August. Onoue, once the largest individual investor in Japan, had used the forged certificates to borrow from a dozen financial institutions. IBJ's Osaka branch had sold her about 290 billion yen of its debentures at the peak and lent about 240 billion yen against them.
imageCaption: Osaka, 2009

headline: IBJ's chairman resigns over the Onoue loans
text: On 22 October IBJ chairman Kaneo Nakamura resigned to take responsibility for 1.85 billion dollars of loans to Nui Onoue; two managing directors and a top adviser also quit and president Yo Kurosawa took a 50% pay cut for six months. 'We are the victims of the scandal but we can't evade our social responsibility,' Nakamura said.
imageCaption: Marunouchi, 2016

headline: A bank run in Thun
text: After local media reported on its finances on 3 October, crowds of depositors rushed to the offices of the Spar- und Leihkasse Thun, a regional bank heavy in mortgages; it is the first notable bank run in Switzerland in decades. Property prices have been falling since 1989, and banks with large property loans are under strain.
imageCaption: Savers queue outside the Spar + Leihkasse Thun to withdraw what they are allowed, October 1991

headline: Exxon pleads guilty and settles Valdez claims for 1 billion
text: On 8 and 9 October a federal judge in Alaska accepted Exxon's guilty plea and a 1.025 billion dollar settlement with the United States and the state of Alaska. Exxon pays 25 million in criminal fines, 100 million in restitution and 900 million over ten years into a fund to restore Prince William Sound. Lawsuits by fishermen and other Alaskans are not covered and continue.
imageCaption: The Exxon Valdez aground in Prince William Sound, Alaska, March 1989

headline: The Soviet Union ceases to exist
text: The leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared on 8 December that the Soviet Union no longer exists and founded a Commonwealth of Independent States, which eight more republics joined on 21 December. Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and handed the nuclear codes to Boris Yeltsin; the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin, and the Soviet Union was formally dissolved the next day.
imageCaption: The heads of eleven former Soviet republics sign the protocol founding the Commonwealth of Independent States, Alma-Ata, December 1991

headline: The Fed cuts sharply and shares end 1991 with an 11 percent burst
text: On 20 December the Federal Reserve cut its discount rate by a full point to 3.5 percent, the lowest in 27 years, to revive a sluggish economy. Shares soared: the Dow set four record closes in a row to end the year at 3,168.83, up 20.3% in 1991, and the S&P 500 rose 11% in December alone to 417.09, up 26% for the year. The recession never quite lifted this year, but falling interest rates lifted the markets. The numbers: the Fed's rate 4.4 percent. Inflation 3.1 percent. Unemployment 7.0 percent.
imageCaption: The Fed's interest rate (blue), inflation (red) and unemployment (grey) in the United States, 1955 to December 1991
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

headline: Maastricht: Europe agrees on a single currency
text: At Maastricht on 9 and 10 December the twelve European Community leaders agreed on a treaty for a European Union with common citizenship, foreign policy cooperation and an economic and monetary union with a single currency by 1999 at the latest. Countries must meet limits on inflation, deficits, debt and interest rates to join. The treaty still has to be ratified by all twelve, some by referendum.
imageCaption: Press conference at the European summit, Maastricht, 11 December 1991

headline: Wal-Mart goes abroad, starting in Mexico
text: In 1991 Wal-Mart formed joint ventures with Cifra, Mexico's largest retailer. The first store, a Club Aurrera warehouse club in Mexico City, opened late this year. Wal-Mart also launched its own label, Sam's American Choice.
imageCaption: A Wal-Mart store in Mexico
